Abstract:
Personalized medicine has the potential to revolutionize the healthcare sector, its goal being to tailor medication to a particular individual by taking into consideration the physiology, drug response, and genetic profile of that individual. There are many technologies emerging to cause this paradigm shift from the conventional “one size fits all” to personalized medicine, the major one being three-dimensional (3D) printing. 3D printing involves the establishment of a three-dimensional object, in a layer upon layer manner using various computer software. 3D printing can be used to construct a wide variety of pharmaceutical dosage forms varying in shape, release profile, and drug combination. The major technological platforms of 3D printing researched on in the pharmaceutical sector include inkjet printing, binder jetting, fused filament fabrication, selective laser sintering, stereolithography, and pressure-assisted microsyringe. A possible future application of this technology could be in a clinical setting, where prescriptions could be dispensed based on individual needs. This manuscript points out the various 3D printing technologies and their applications in research for fabricating pharmaceutical products, along with their pros and cons. It also presents its potential in personalized medicine by individualizing the dose, release profiles, and incorporating multiple drugs in a polypill. An insight on how it tends to various populations is also provided. An approach of how it can be used in a clinical setting is also highlighted. Also, various challenges faced are pointed out, which must be overcome for the success of this technology in personalized medicine.

Abstract:
Background/Objectives: The pharmacy profession has undergone significant changes driven by advancements in patient care and healthcare systems. The FDA approval of Spritam® (levetiracetam), the first 3D-printed drug, has sparked increased interest in the use of Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D printing for pharmaceutical applications, particularly in the production of polypills. Methods: This review provides an overview of FDM 3D printing in the development of pharmaceutical dosage forms, focusing on its operation, printing parameters, materials, additives, advantages, and limitations. Key aspects, such as the ability to personalize medication and the challenges associated with the technique, including drug stability at high temperatures, are discussed. Results: Fourteen studies relevant to FDM 3D-printed polypills were analyzed from an initial pool of 60. The increasing number of publications highlights the growing global interest in this technology, with the UK contributing the highest number of studies. Conclusions: FDM 3D printing offers significant potential for personalized medicine by enabling precise control over dosage forms and tailoring treatments to individual patient needs. However, limitations such as high printing temperatures and the lack of standardized GMP guidelines for large-scale production must be addressed to fully realize its potential in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Objectives: Personalized medicine is gaining rapid attention over the current drug prescription approach of ‘one-size-fits-all’. Three-dimensional (3D) printing is one such product development technique that has the potential to transform the pharmaceutical and biomedical sectors. Methods: To establish the future of 3D printing in mainstream pharmacy practice, initially, pharmaceutical preclinical and clinical scientific databases (peer-reviewed articles, patents, and marketed products) over the past 10 years were critically scrutinized. Additionally, to provide context, we developed a hypothetical case study illustrating the capabilities of the 3D printing super-compounding pharmacy in personalized patient care, emphasizing the critical role of pharmacists in this process. Results: Acknowledging the potential of 3D printing in pharmacy practice, this review effectively summarizes the advances and opportunities of pharmaceutically feasible 3D printing methods, as well as the challenges in translating this technology into a future super-compounding pharmacy facility. Furthermore, the review highlights the promising capabilities of such pharmaceutical 3D printers in enabling on-site printing of 3D medicines tailored to individual needs, which may range from dose adjustments to multidrug single tablets (polypills). Conclusions: We believe that 3D printing technology has the potential to revolutionize precision and personalized medication approaches in pharmacy practice, which will significantly benefit patient healthcare outcomes. Additionally, the adoption of such technology in pharmacies will lead to a reinvention of the role of pharmacists, thereby creating more job opportunities. Ultimately, 3D printing will create a new paradigm of super-compounding pharmacy practice, providing a new sense of excitement for those looking to enter the pharmacy profession.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This work aimed to develop a three-dimensional printed (3DP) tablet containing glimepiride (GLMP) and/or rosuvastatin (RSV) for treatment of dyslipidemia in patients with diabetes. Curcumin oil was extracted from the dried rhizomes of Curcuma longa and utilized to develop a self-nanoemulsifying drug delivery system (SNEDDS). Screening mixture experimental design was conducted to develop SNEDDS formulation with a minimum droplet size. Five different semi-solid pastes were prepared and rheologically characterized. The prepared pastes were used to develop 3DP tablets using extrusion printing. The quality attributes of the 3DP tablets were evaluated. A non-compartmental extravascular pharmacokinetic model was implemented to investigate the in vivo behavior of the prepared tablets and the studied marketed products. The optimized SNEDDS, of a 94.43 ± 3.55 nm droplet size, was found to contain 15%, 75%, and 10% of oil, polyethylene glycol 400, and tween 80, respectively. The prepared pastes revealed a shear-thinning of pseudoplastic flow behavior. Flat-faced round tablets of 15 mm diameter and 5.6–11.2 mm thickness were successfully printed and illustrated good criteria for friability, weight variation, and content uniformity. Drug release was superior from SNEDDS-based tablets when compared to non-SNEDDS tablets. Scanning electron microscopy study of the 3DP tablets revealed a semi-porous surface that exhibited some curvature with the appearance of tortuosity and a gel porous-like structure of the inner section. GLMP and RSV demonstrated relative bioavailability of 159.50% and 245.16%, respectively. Accordingly, the developed 3DP tablets could be considered as a promising combined oral drug therapy used in treatment of metabolic disorders. However, clinical studies are needed to investigate their efficacy and safety.

Abstract:
Fragment-based screening has evolved as a remarkable approach within the drug discovery process both in the industry and academia. Fragment screening has become a more structure-based approach to inhibitor development, but also towards development of pathway-specific clinical probes. However, it is often witnessed that the availability, immediate and long-term, of a high quality fragment-screening library is still beyond the reach of most academic laboratories. Within iNEXT (Infrastructure for NMR, EM and X-rays for Translational research), a EU-funded Horizon 2020 program, a collection of 782 fragments were assembled utilizing the concept of “poised fragments” with the aim to facilitate downstream synthesis of ligands with high affinity by fragment ligation. Herein, we describe the analytical procedure to assess the quality of this purchased and assembled fragment library by NMR spectroscopy. This quality assessment requires buffer solubility screening, comparison with LC/MS quality control and is supported by state-of-the-art software for high throughput data acquisition and on-the-fly data analysis. Results from the analysis of the library are presented as a prototype of fragment progression through the quality control process.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In any biomedical and chemical context, a truthful description of chemical constitution requires coverage of both structure and purity. This qualification affects all drug molecules, regardless of development stage (early discovery to approved drug) and source (natural product or synthetic). Purity assessment is particularly critical in discovery programs and whenever chemistry is linked with biological and/or therapeutic outcome. Compared with chromatography and elemental analysis, quantitative NMR (qNMR) uses nearly universal detection and provides a versatile and orthogonal means of purity evaluation. Absolute qNMR with flexible calibration captures analytes that frequently escape detection (water, sorbents). Widely accepted structural NMR workflows require minimal or no adjustments to become practical 1H qNMR (qHNMR) procedures with simultaneous qualitative and (absolute) quantitative capability. This study reviews underlying concepts, provides a framework for standard qHNMR purity assays, and shows how adequate accuracy and precision are achieved for the intended use of the material.</jats:p>

Automated solid-powder dispensing for medicinal-chemistry HTE must deliver small, reproducible doses across 96- and 384-well formats, while avoiding powder-flow problems such as bridging, static buildup, clogging, jamming, and inconsistent dosing. Conventional automated robots can provide sub-milligram accuracy and have demonstrated relative standard deviations typically below 5% across 96-well plates, but they may require substantial capital investment and laboratory space, and equipment malfunctions can cause downtime. ChemBeads address these issues by attaching uniformly distributed solid reagents to spherical, chemically inert glass beads. Their consistent physical properties and high flowability support reliable volumetric dispensing and help prevent common powder-handling failures. Automated platforms can dose multiple ChemBeads into microplates, including 96- and 384-well formats. For laboratories without robotic systems, calibrated fixed- or variable-volume scoops provide reproducible manual dosing without balance-based weighing; the delivered active amount can be calculated from pre-characterized loading. A parallel dispenser offers a lower-cost, higher-throughput alternative, using 96 calibrated holes designed for 3 mg of ChemBeads and achieving an error margin of ±5%. Multiple dispensers or premixed bead formulations can support dispensing multiple reagents per vial.

This is especially problematic when HTE requires representative neat powders or solid dosage forms for formulation, solubility, and solid-form studies. Commercial precision powder-handling systems can improve accuracy, but their cost, maintenance, and footprint restrict adoption; slurry dosing, wax encapsulation, capsules, and tablets have additional problems such as uneven distribution, clogging, or reagent degradation. ChemBeads address the problem by dry-coating finely powdered active reagents onto chemically inert glass beads, standardizing physical handling properties without compromising chemical integrity. The resulting free-flowing formulations support accurate, reproducible volumetric dispensing with standard robotic or manual tools, from nanomole to milligram scales. Bead surface area, size, and loading must be selected carefully: surface area controls capacity, while bead size supports uniform flow and prevents clogging. Typical loading is 0.5–20% w/w; approximately 5% w/w generally balances flowability, homogeneity, and automated dispense range.

Abstract:
Background Open source drug discovery offers potential for developing new and inexpensive drugs to combat diseases that disproportionally affect the poor. The concept borrows two principle aspects from open source computing (i.e., collaboration and open access) and applies them to pharmaceutical innovation. By opening a project to external contributors, its research capacity may increase significantly. To date there are only a handful of open source R&D projects focusing on neglected diseases. We wanted to learn from these first movers, their successes and failures, in order to generate a better understanding of how a much-discussed theoretical concept works in practice and may be implemented. Methodology/Principal Findings A descriptive case study was performed, evaluating two specific R&D projects focused on neglected diseases. CSIR Team India Consortium's Open Source Drug Discovery project (CSIR OSDD) and The Synaptic Leap's Schistosomiasis project (TSLS). Data were gathered from four sources: interviews of participating members (n = 14), a survey of potential members (n = 61), an analysis of the websites and a literature review. Both cases have made significant achievements; however, they have done so in very different ways. CSIR OSDD encourages international collaboration, but its process facilitates contributions from mostly Indian researchers and students. Its processes are formal with each task being reviewed by a mentor (almost always offline) before a result is made public. TSLS, on the other hand, has attracted contributors internationally, albeit significantly fewer than CSIR OSDD. Both have obtained funding used to pay for access to facilities, physical resources and, at times, labor costs. TSLS releases its results into the public domain, whereas CSIR OSDD asserts ownership over its results. Conclusions/Significance Technically TSLS is an open source project, whereas CSIR OSDD is a crowdsourced project. However, both have enabled high quality research at low cost. The critical success factors appear to be clearly defined entry points, transparency and funding to cover core material costs.

Abstract:
Early disease diagnosis is necessary to enable timely interventions. Implementation of this vital task in the developing world is challenging owing to limited resources. Diagnostic approaches developed for resource-limited settings have often involved colorimetric tests (based on immunoassays) due to their low cost. Unfortunately, the performance/sensitivity of such simplistic tests are often limited and significantly hinder opportunities for early disease detection. A new criterion for selecting diagnostic tests in low- and middle-income countries is proposed here that is based on performance-to-cost ratio. For example, modern mass spectrometry (MS) now involves analysis of the native sample in the open laboratory environment, enabling applications in many fields, including clinical research, forensic science, environmental analysis, and agriculture. In this critical review, we summarize recent developments in chemistry that enable MS to be applied effectively in developing countries. In particular, we argue that closed automated analytical systems may not offer the analytical flexibility needed in resource-limited settings. Alternative strategies proposed here have potential to be widely accepted in low- and middle-income countries through the utilization of the open-source ambient MS platform that enables microsampling techniques such as dried blood spot to be coupled with miniature mass spectrometers in a centralized analytical platform. Consequently, costs associated with sample handling and maintenance can be reduced by >50% of the total ownership cost, permitting analytical measurements to be operated at high performance-to-cost ratios in the developing world. Abstract:
Protocols in the academic life science laboratory are heavily reliant on the manual manipulation of tools, reagents and instruments by a host of research staff and students. In contrast to industrial and clinical laboratory environments, the usage of automation to augment or replace manual tasks is limited. Causes of this ‘automation gap’ are unique to academic research, with rigid short-term funding structures, high levels of protocol variability and a benevolent culture of investment in people over equipment. Automation, however, can bestow multiple benefits through improvements in reproducibility, researcher efficiency, clinical translation, and safety. Less immediately obvious are the accompanying limitations, including obsolescence and an inhibitory effect on the freedom to innovate. Growing the range of automation options suitable for research laboratories will require more flexible, modular and cheaper designs. Academic and commercial developers of automation will increasingly need to design with an environmental awareness and an understanding that large high-tech robotic solutions may not be appropriate for laboratories with constrained financial and spatial resources. To fully exploit the potential of laboratory automation, future generations of scientists will require both engineering and biology skills. Automation in the research laboratory is likely to be an increasingly critical component of future research programs and will continue the trend of combining engineering and science expertise together to answer novel research questions.

Abstract:
There is an urgent need to make drug discovery cheaper and faster. This will enable the development of treatments for diseases currently neglected for economic reasons, such as tropical and orphan diseases, and generally increase the supply of new drugs. Here, we report the Robot Scientist ‘Eve’ designed to make drug discovery more economical. A Robot Scientist is a laboratory automation system that uses artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to discover scientific knowledge through cycles of experimentation. Eve integrates and automates library-screening, hit-confirmation, and lead generation through cycles of quantitative structure activity relationship learning and testing. Using econometric modelling we demonstrate that the use of AI to select compounds economically outperforms standard drug screening. For further efficiency Eve uses a standardized form of assay to compute Boolean functions of compound properties. These assays can be quickly and cheaply engineered using synthetic biology, enabling more targets to be assayed for a given budget. Eve has repositioned several drugs against specific targets in parasites that cause tropical diseases. One validated discovery is that the anti-cancer compound TNP-470 is a potent inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase from the malaria-causing parasite Plasmodium vivax.

Abstract:
Falsified and substandard drugs are a global health problem, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) that have weak pharmacovigilance and drug regulatory systems. Poor quality medicines have important health consequences, including the potential for treatment failure, development of antimicrobial resistance, and serious adverse drug reactions, increasing healthcare costs and undermining the public's confidence in healthcare systems. This article presents a review of the methods employed for the analysis of pharmaceutical formulations. Technologies for detecting substandard and falsified drugs were identified primarily through literature reviews. Key-informant interviews with experts augmented our methods when warranted. In order to aid comparisons, technologies were assigned a suitability score for use in LMIC ranging from 0–8. Scores measured the need for electricity, need for sample preparation, need for reagents, portability, level of training required, and speed of analysis. Technologies with higher scores were deemed the most feasible in LMICs. We categorized technologies that cost $10,000 USD or less as low cost, $10,000–100,000 USD as medium cost and those greater than $100,000 USD as high cost technologies (all prices are 2013 USD). This search strategy yielded information on 42 unique technologies. Five technologies were deemed both low cost and had feasibility scores between 6–8, and an additional four technologies had medium cost and high feasibility. Twelve technologies were deemed portable and therefore could be used in the field. Many technologies can aid in the detection of substandard and falsified drugs that vary from the simplest of checklists for packaging to the most complex mass spectrometry analyses. Although there is no single technology that can serve all the requirements of detecting falsified and substandard drugs, there is an opportunity to bifurcate the technologies into specific niches to address specific sections within the workflow process of detecting products.

Abstract:
Respiratory diseases pose an increasing socio-economic burden worldwide given their high prevalence and their elevated morbidity and mortality. Medical devices play an important role in managing acute and chronic respiratory failure, including diagnosis, monitoring, and providing artificial ventilation. Current commercially available respiratory devices are very effective but, given their cost, are unaffordable for most patients in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Herein, we focus on a relatively new design option—the open-source hardware approach—that, if implemented, will contribute to providing low-cost respiratory medical devices for many patients in LMICs, particularly those without full medical insurance coverage. Open source reflects a set of approaches to conceive and distribute the comprehensive technical information required for building devices. The open-source approach enables free and unrestricted use of the know-how to replicate and manufacture the device or modify its design for improvements or adaptation to different clinical settings or personalized treatments. We describe recent examples of open-source devices for diagnosis/monitoring (measuring inspiratory/expiratory pressures or flow and volume in mechanical ventilators) and for therapy (non-invasive ventilators for adults and continuous positive airway pressure support for infants) that enable building simple, low-cost (hence, affordable), and high-performance solutions for patients in LMICs. Finally, we argue that the common practice of approving clinical trials by the local hospital ethics board can be expanded to ensure patient safety by reviewing, inspecting, and approving open hardware for medical application to maximize the innovation and deployment rate of medical technologies.

Abstract:
Background Substandard and falsified medical products present a serious threat to public health, especially in low- and middle-income countries. Their identification using pharmacopeial analysis is expensive and requires sophisticated equipment and highly trained personnel. Simple, low-cost technologies are required in addition to full pharmacopeial analysis in order to accomplish widespread routine surveillance for poor-quality medicines in low- and middle-income countries. Methods Ten faith-based drug supply organizations in seven countries of Africa and Asia were each equipped with a Minilab of the Global Pharma Health Fund (GPHF, Frankfurt, Germany), suitable for the analysis of about 85 different essential medicines by thin-layer chromatography. Each organization was asked to collect approximately 100 medicine samples from private local medicine outlets, especially from the informal sector. The medicine samples were tested locally according to the Minilab protocols. Medicines which failed Minilab testing were subjected to confirmatory analysis in a WHO-prequalified medicine quality control laboratory in Kenya. Results Out of 869 medicine samples, 21 were confirmed to be substandard or falsified medical products. Twelve did not contain the stated active pharmaceutical ingredient (API), six contained insufficient amounts of the API, and three showed insufficient dissolution of the API. The highest proportion of substandard and falsified medicines was found in Cameroon (7.1%), followed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (2.7%) and Nigeria (1.1%). Antimalarial medicines were most frequently found to be substandard or falsified (9.5% of all antimalarials). Thin-layer chromatography according to the Minilab protocols was found to be specific and reproducible in the identification of medicines which did not contain the stated API. Since only samples which failed Minilab testing were subjected to confirmatory testing using pharmacopeial methods, this study did not assess the sensitivity of the Minilab methodology in the detection of substandard medicines, and may underestimate the prevalence of poor-quality medicines. Conclusions Surveillance for poor-quality medicines can be carried out by local organizations in low- and middle-income countries using a simple, low-cost technology. Such surveillance can identify an important subgroup of the circulating substandard and falsified medical products and can help to prevent them from causing harm in patients. A collaboration of the national drug regulatory authorities with faith-based organizations and other NGOs may therefore represent a promising strategy towards the Sustainable Development Goal of “ensuring access to quality medicines”.

Abstract:
In this review, we examine the current landscape of point-of-care testing (POCT) diagnostic tools designed for poverty-related infectious diseases (PRIDs) in sub-Saharan Africa (sSA) while delineating key avenues for future advancements. Our analysis encompasses both established and emerging diagnostic methods for PRIDs, addressing the persistent challenges in POCT tool development and deployment, such as cost, accessibility, and reliability. We emphasize recent advancements in POCT diagnostic tools as well as platforms poised to enhance diagnostic testing in sSA. Recognizing the urgency for affordable and widely accessible POCT diagnostic tools to detect PRIDs in sSA, we advocate for a multidisciplinary approach. This approach integrates current and emerging diagnostic methods, explicitly addressing challenges hindering point-of-care (POC) tool development. Furthermore, it recognizes the profound impact of misdiagnosis on public and global health, emphasizing the need for effective tools. To facilitate the successful development and implementation of POCT diagnostic tools in sSA, we propose strategies including the creation of multi-analyte detection POCT tools, the implementation of education and training programs, community engagement initiatives, fostering public-private collaborations, and the establishment of reliable supply chains. Through these concerted efforts, we aim to accelerate the development of POCT in the sSA region, ensuring its effectiveness and accessibility in addressing the diagnostic challenges associated with PRIDs.

Amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) are among the most popular and widely studied solubility enhancement techniques. Abstract:
Amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) offer a well-recognized strategy to improve the effective solubility and, hence, bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs. In this study, we developed an extensive library of a significant number of solid dispersion formulations using a library of chemically diverse drugs combined with a water-soluble polymer (polyvinylpyrrolidone vinyl acetate, PVPVA) at different loadings. These formulations were printed as microarrays of solid dispersion formulations, utilizing minimal material amounts (nanograms). They were subjected to a six-month stability study under accelerated conditions (40 °C and 75% relative humidity). Physical stability outcomes varied significantly among the different drug–polymer combinations, with stability ranging from immediate drug crystallization to several days of stability. The comprehensive data set obtained from this high-throughput screening was used to construct multiple linear regression models to correlate the stability of ASDs with the physicochemical properties of the used Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs). Our findings reveal that increased stability of ASDs is associated with a lower number of hydrogen bond acceptors alongside a higher overall count of heteroatoms and oxygen atoms in the drug molecules. This suggests that, while heteroatoms and oxygen are abundant, their role as hydrogen bond acceptors is limited due to their specific chemical environments, contributing to overall stability. Additionally, drugs with lower melting points formed more stable ASDs within the polymer matrix. This study, hence, highlights the importance of minimizing repulsive drug–polymer interactions to yield a physically stable ASD. The developed models, validated through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation, demonstrated good predictability of stability trends. Hence, the high-throughput 2D inkjet printing technique that was used to manufacture the microarrays proved valuable for assessing drug–polymer crystallization onset risks and predicting stability outcomes. In conclusion, this study demonstrates a novel approach to solid dispersion formulation physical stability screening, enhancing efficiency, minimizing material requirements, and expanding the range of samples evaluated. Our findings provide insights into the critical physicochemical properties influencing ASD stability, offering a significant advancement in developing stable ASDs.

Solid-powder handling is a major motor-function challenge for self-driving laboratories because automated systems have difficulty accurately dispensing small quantities, particularly when powders have substantially different physical properties. The excerpt identifies amounts below approximately 20 mg as especially problematic. Achieving the required performance means obtaining both accuracy and precision, which requires substantial calibration and testing. This becomes difficult in discovery-mode synthesis, where hundreds of different solids may each need customized dispensing settings, making comprehensive calibration impractical. The excerpt does not provide a numerical tolerance or a specific accuracy percentage; it only states that both accuracy and precision are required. Current SDLs commonly avoid direct powder dispensing by using stock solutions and established liquid-handling technologies, enabling procedures to be scaled down accurately. Stock-solution preparation itself can be automated using computer vision. More broadly, heterogeneous mixtures also create problems for pump-based liquid-transfer systems because they can damage or malfunction, and purification systems such as solid-phase extraction cartridges may suffer blockages and leaks that require human intervention. Thus, SDL designs generally favor liquid formulations and careful monitoring, while direct solid handling remains an area needing improved hardware, calibration, and flexibility.

Abstract:
Abstract High throughput experimentation is a growing and evolving field that allows to execute dozens to several thousands of experiments per day with relatively limited resources. Through miniaturization, typically a high degree of automation and the use of digital data tools, many parallel reactions or experiments at a time can be run in such workflows. High throughput experimentation also requires fast analytical techniques capable of generating critically important analytical data in line with the increased rate of experimentation. As traditional techniques usually do not deliver the speed required, some unique approaches are required to enable workflows to function as designed. This review covers the recent developments (2019‐2020) in this field and was intended to give a comprehensive overview of the current “state‐of‐the‐art.”

Abstract:
Positron emission tomography is a widely used imaging platform for studying physiological processes. Despite the proliferation of modern synthetic methodologies for radiolabeling, the optimization of these reactions still primarily relies on inefficient one-factor-at-a-time approaches. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) has proven to be a powerful approach for optimizing reactions in many areas of chemical synthesis. However, to date, HTE has rarely been applied to radiochemistry. This is largely because of the short lifetime of common radioisotopes, which presents major challenges for efficient parallel reaction setup and analysis using standard equipment and workflows. Herein, we demonstrate an effective HTE workflow and apply it to the optimization of copper-mediated radiofluorination of pharmaceutically relevant boronate ester substrates. The workflow utilizes commercial equipment and allows for rapid analysis of reactions for optimizing reactions, exploring chemical space using pharmaceutically relevant aryl boronates for radiofluorinations, and constructing large radiochemistry data sets.

{"answer": "## Application Opportunities for an Open-Source Gravimetric Powder Doser in Drug Discovery and Pharmaceutical R&D

### 1. Overview and Central Value Proposition

The proposed open-source gravimetric powder doser, operating in the milligram-to-gram range with load-cell feedback, is well positioned to serve as the upstream "solid-to-stock-solution" conversion module across multiple pharmaceutical R&D workflows. A critical insight from the literature is that **when the exact dispensed mass is recorded and solvent volume is adjusted to reach the target concentration, the stringency of gravimetric precision requirements is substantially relaxed**. Validated quantitative ¹H NMR (qNMR) methods achieve approximately 1% repeatability and 2% accuracy for concentration verification of DMSO stock solutions (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). When concentration is independently verified by qNMR, chemiluminescent nitrogen detection (CLND), or LC-UV/MS, the analytical method becomes the controlling concentration assignment, so that even ±5–10% dispensing accuracy is acceptable provided the actual mass is logged and the stock concentration is either corrected or analytically reassigned (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). This architecture—weigh, record, dissolve, verify—decouples the performance floor of the powder doser from the precision ceiling demanded by downstream nanoliter-to-picoliter liquid dispensing.

The following sections evaluate six application domains, summarized in the comparison table below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 2. Application-by-Application Evaluation

#### 2.1 Stock-Solution Preparation for Cell-Based, Microfluidic and Organ-on-Chip Drug Sensitivity Assays

Drug screening libraries are routinely prepared as nominal 10 mM DMSO stock solutions from which small aliquots are dispensed into assay plates (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000046). The upstream step—weighing a few milligrams of compound into a vial and adding DMSO—is typically manual, slow, and a well-documented source of error. Compound precipitation from DMSO stocks affects approximately 26% of wells in some diversity libraries, producing substantial concentration discrepancies between nominal and actual molarity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046). An automated gravimetric doser dispensing 1–20 mg of API into barcode-tracked vials, followed by automated solvent addition calibrated to the actual recorded mass, would directly address this bottleneck. The resulting verified mother stocks would feed acoustic dispensers, pin-tool devices, or microfluidic concentration-gradient generators supplying organ-on-chip, tumor-on-chip and personalized oncology assays. Milligram resolution is fully sufficient; sub-milligram capability is unnecessary unless compounds are exceptionally scarce or high-potency.

**Required specifications:** 1–20 mg dose range; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; moderate throughput (~10–100 vials/day); no GMP requirements for research stocks; barcode tracking and automated solvent-volume correction.

#### 2.2 Solid-Form and Pre-Formulation Screening

High-throughput polymorph screening commonly uses 1–3 mg of API per crystallization condition, with total campaign consumption of less than 5 g for approximately 1,500 conditions (pqac-00000019). Salt-selection screens can be conducted with less than 200 mg of total API across 150–200 experiments (pqac-00000021), while cocrystal discovery using jet-dispensing HTS has been demonstrated with less than 50 mg of starting material (pqac-00000023). Powder-dispersion solubility assays operate at 0.1–15 mg per well (pqac-00000022), and solvent-cast miniaturized screening uses 10–40 µg per formulation (pqac-00000024). The doser is well suited for preparing individual crystallization charges (1–15 mg), master stock solutions for solubility screening, and accurately weighed API–coformer mixtures at controlled stoichiometric ratios. It does not address nanogram-scale inkjet or nanospot approaches (pqac-00000020), but these represent specialized miniaturized platforms rather than routine workflows.

**Required specifications:** 1–15 mg per vial; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; 96 vials/batch; humidity control option to protect hygroscopic forms; low-shear dispensing that does not transform the solid.

#### 2.3 High-Throughput Experimentation for Medicinal and Process Chemistry

Solid-powder dispensing remains a major bottleneck in pharmaceutical HTE (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009). Miniaturized HTE reactions typically require 0.25–1 mg per catalyst/ligand component and may operate at 0.1–4 µmol or even nanomole scales (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). At these scales, native powder properties—variable bulk density, electrostatic charging, hygroscopicity and poor flow—cause inconsistent dosing and instrument stalls (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Commercial dispensing platforms including Chemspeed FLEX/SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and Unchained Labs systems can handle sub-milligram quantities but cannot deliver nanomole amounts with acceptable error (pqac-00000049). The ChemBeads approach addresses this by coating reagents onto glass beads, achieving ±5% accuracy at 20 mg targets and enabling dispensing into 96- and 384-well plates (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048).

The gravimetric doser fits this space primarily as an **upstream stock-solution and slurry preparation tool** rather than as a direct miniaturized-reaction dispenser. For conventional vial-scale screens using 5–50 mg of bases, oxidants and stoichiometric reagents, direct dispensing is feasible. Sub-milligram capability would be needed for true miniaturized HTE, which is outside the doser's core operating range.

**Required specifications for stock/slurry preparation:** 5–100 mg; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; rapid powder changeover; inert-atmosphere option.

#### 2.4 Formulation and Drug-Product Prototyping

3D-printed tablets and capsule prototypes typically contain milligrams to grams of API per unit. Dry-powder inhaler (DPI) development spans approximately 0.5–500 mg fill mass, with demonstrated performance of <2.3% RSD at 10 mg and <0.8% RSD at optimized conditions using dosator equipment (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). At the low end (~0.5 mg), fill-weight variability can reach 11% RSD (pqac-00000030), highlighting the challenge of low-dose powder fills. Personalized compounding and 3D-printed medicine require accurate, recipe-driven API dosing with traceability, but regulatory frameworks for 3D-printed dosage forms remain under development (pqac-00000027). For aseptic pharmaceutical applications, equipment must tolerate aggressive decontamination, use pharmaceutical-grade contact materials, and operate within validated environments (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031).

The doser is well suited for R&D prototyping—blend preparation, capsule charges, and printer feedstock dispensing at 10 mg–2 g—but GMP manufacture of clinical or patient-supplied material would require equipment qualification, validated cleaning, content-uniformity testing and regulatory compliance beyond what an open-source research tool typically provides.

**Required specifications:** 10 mg–2 g; ±0.5 mg readability; ≤3% RSD; recipe-driven multi-powder operation; cleaning-validation potential; lot traceability.

#### 2.5 Self-Driving and Autonomous Chemistry Laboratories

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) commonly avoid direct powder dispensing, instead preparing stock solutions to convert the problem into established liquid handling (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). The difficulty of accurately dispensing amounts below approximately 20 mg is explicitly identified as a motor-function limitation (pqac-00000008), and solid-dispensing hardware is described as comparatively rare and expensive (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038). Commercial special-purpose SDL hardware costs approximately $1 million, while open hardware ranges from $100 to $2,000 (pqac-00000034). The gravimetric doser would close a recognized gap by autonomously converting powders into robot-compatible, concentration-verified stock solutions, enabling SDLs to expand their reagent scope without requiring direct sub-milligram powder delivery into reaction vessels.

**Required specifications:** 5–500 mg; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; unattended 24/7 operation with error recovery; open scheduling API; auditable metadata; enclosures and interlocks.

#### 2.6 Academic Core Facilities and Low-Resource Laboratories

The cost barrier to automated powder dispensing is substantial. Commercial liquid-handling workstations cost approximately $50,000–$60,000 (pqac-00000036), while specialized powder-dispensing systems from Chemspeed, Mettler-Toledo and similar manufacturers require "substantial capital investment" with additional costs for maintenance, laboratory space, and proprietary consumables (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000050). In contrast, open-source laboratory automation platforms have been demonstrated at costs ranging from $335 for 3-axis autosamplers to $900 for microbalance-autosampler systems and under $500 for complete 3D-printed scientific platforms (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035). A documented, open-source powder doser at less than $5,000 BOM would represent a 10–100× cost reduction relative to commercial alternatives, democratizing a capability that remains uncommon in academic laboratories and virtually absent in low-resource settings.

**Required specifications:** 1 mg–5 g; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; simple calibration and maintenance; locally replaceable contact parts; open-source documentation, BOM, software and validation protocols.

---

### 3. Accuracy Requirements When Mass Is Recorded and Concentration Verified

A central question for the doser's value proposition is whether milligram-level gravimetric resolution is sufficient when downstream concentration correction is applied. The evidence strongly supports an affirmative answer for all six applications, with important caveats:

- **Gravimetric mass recording with solvent adjustment:** When the actual dispensed mass is recorded and solvent volume is calculated to reach the target molarity, preparation errors become traceable rather than unknown. The accuracy requirement shifts from "hit the target mass precisely" to "record the actual mass precisely" (pqac-00000016). A balance with 0.1 mg readability and ≤5% RSD dispensing performance is sufficient for this architecture.

- **Post-preparation concentration verification:** qNMR provides absolute concentration measurement with approximately 1% precision and 2% accuracy (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). LC-UV/MS relative purity can substantially misrepresent actual strength because it assumes all peaks sum to 100% (pqac-00000016). When qNMR or CLND is used for post-preparation verification, even larger initial dispensing errors are tolerable because the analytical measurement supersedes the gravimetric estimate.

- **The dominant source of error is not weighing:** Compound precipitation from DMSO stocks—observed in 26% of wells in one library study—can produce concentration errors of 50% or more (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047). Dissolution and stability therefore matter more than milligram-level weighing precision, and the doser should incorporate dissolution verification (visual, turbidimetric or spectroscopic) as part of the workflow.

---

### 4. Ranked Priority List and Key Performance Specifications

The following table ranks the six application niches by technical fit, addressable user base, and strategic value for an open-source milligram-to-gram gravimetric doser, and provides consolidated cross-application target specifications.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

---

### 5. Conclusions

The open-source gravimetric powder doser occupies a well-defined and underserved niche in pharmaceutical R&D automation: the **solid-to-stock-solution conversion** step that bridges bulk compound storage and downstream nanoliter-to-picoliter liquid dispensing. Its milligram-to-gram operating range directly matches the most common stock-preparation, pre-formulation and prototyping workflows. The key enabling insight is that gravimetric feedback with mass recording, followed by solvent-volume adjustment or analytical concentration verification, relaxes the accuracy requirement from the sub-milligram level demanded by direct miniaturized reaction dosing to the ±5% level readily achievable by auger/vibratory gravimetric systems. The doser does not compete with commercial sub-milligram platforms or ChemBead technology for direct 96/384-well HTE reaction setup, but it fills the upstream preparation gap that these platforms and self-driving laboratories currently address manually or avoid entirely. At a target BOM of less than $5,000, the open-source doser would represent a 10–100× cost reduction relative to commercial alternatives, making automated powder handling accessible to academic core facilities, low-resource laboratories and modular SDL architectures worldwide."}

#### 2.1 Stock-Solution Preparation for Cell-Based, Microfluidic and Organ-on-Chip Drug Sensitivity Assays

Drug screening libraries are routinely prepared as nominal 10 mM DMSO stock solutions from which small aliquots are dispensed into assay plates (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000046). The upstream step—weighing a few milligrams of compound into a vial and adding DMSO—is typically manual, slow, and a well-documented source of error. Compound precipitation from DMSO stocks affects approximately 26% of wells in some diversity libraries, producing substantial concentration discrepancies between nominal and actual molarity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046). An automated gravimetric doser dispensing 1–20 mg of API into barcode-tracked vials, followed by automated solvent addition calibrated to the actual recorded mass, would directly address this bottleneck. The resulting verified mother stocks would feed acoustic dispensers, pin-tool devices, or microfluidic concentration-gradient generators supplying organ-on-chip, tumor-on-chip and personalized oncology assays. Milligram resolution is fully sufficient; sub-milligram capability is unnecessary unless compounds are exceptionally scarce or high-potency.

**Required specifications:** 1–20 mg dose range; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; moderate throughput (~10–100 vials/day); no GMP requirements for research stocks; barcode tracking and automated solvent-volume correction.

#### 2.2 Solid-Form and Pre-Formulation Screening

High-throughput polymorph screening commonly uses 1–3 mg of API per crystallization condition, with total campaign consumption of less than 5 g for approximately 1,500 conditions (pqac-00000019). Salt-selection screens can be conducted with less than 200 mg of total API across 150–200 experiments (pqac-00000021), while cocrystal discovery using jet-dispensing HTS has been demonstrated with less than 50 mg of starting material (pqac-00000023). Powder-dispersion solubility assays operate at 0.1–15 mg per well (pqac-00000022), and solvent-cast miniaturized screening uses 10–40 µg per formulation (pqac-00000024). The doser is well suited for preparing individual crystallization charges (1–15 mg), master stock solutions for solubility screening, and accurately weighed API–coformer mixtures at controlled stoichiometric ratios. It does not address nanogram-scale inkjet or nanospot approaches (pqac-00000020), but these represent specialized miniaturized platforms rather than routine workflows.

**Required specifications:** 1–15 mg per vial; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; 96 vials/batch; humidity control option to protect hygroscopic forms; low-shear dispensing that does not transform the solid.

#### 2.3 High-Throughput Experimentation for Medicinal and Process Chemistry

Solid-powder dispensing remains a major bottleneck in pharmaceutical HTE (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009). Miniaturized HTE reactions typically require 0.25–1 mg per catalyst/ligand component and may operate at 0.1–4 µmol or even nanomole scales (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). At these scales, native powder properties—variable bulk density, electrostatic charging, hygroscopicity and poor flow—cause inconsistent dosing and instrument stalls (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). Commercial dispensing platforms including Chemspeed FLEX/SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and Unchained Labs systems can handle sub-milligram quantities but cannot deliver nanomole amounts with acceptable error (pqac-00000049). The ChemBeads approach addresses this by coating reagents onto glass beads, achieving ±5% accuracy at 20 mg targets and enabling dispensing into 96- and 384-well plates (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048).

The gravimetric doser fits this space primarily as an **upstream stock-solution and slurry preparation tool** rather than as a direct miniaturized-reaction dispenser. For conventional vial-scale screens using 5–50 mg of bases, oxidants and stoichiometric reagents, direct dispensing is feasible. Sub-milligram capability would be needed for true miniaturized HTE, which is outside the doser's core operating range.

**Required specifications for stock/slurry preparation:** 5–100 mg; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; rapid powder changeover; inert-atmosphere option.

#### 2.4 Formulation and Drug-Product Prototyping

3D-printed tablets and capsule prototypes typically contain milligrams to grams of API per unit. Dry-powder inhaler (DPI) development spans approximately 0.5–500 mg fill mass, with demonstrated performance of <2.3% RSD at 10 mg and <0.8% RSD at optimized conditions using dosator equipment (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). At the low end (~0.5 mg), fill-weight variability can reach 11% RSD (pqac-00000030), highlighting the challenge of low-dose powder fills. Personalized compounding and 3D-printed medicine require accurate, recipe-driven API dosing with traceability, but regulatory frameworks for 3D-printed dosage forms remain under development (pqac-00000027). For aseptic pharmaceutical applications, equipment must tolerate aggressive decontamination, use pharmaceutical-grade contact materials, and operate within validated environments (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031).

The doser is well suited for R&D prototyping—blend preparation, capsule charges, and printer feedstock dispensing at 10 mg–2 g—but GMP manufacture of clinical or patient-supplied material would require equipment qualification, validated cleaning, content-uniformity testing and regulatory compliance beyond what an open-source research tool typically provides.

**Required specifications:** 10 mg–2 g; ±0.5 mg readability; ≤3% RSD; recipe-driven multi-powder operation; cleaning-validation potential; lot traceability.

#### 2.5 Self-Driving and Autonomous Chemistry Laboratories

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) commonly avoid direct powder dispensing, instead preparing stock solutions to convert the problem into established liquid handling (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). The difficulty of accurately dispensing amounts below approximately 20 mg is explicitly identified as a motor-function limitation (pqac-00000008), and solid-dispensing hardware is described as comparatively rare and expensive (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038). Commercial special-purpose SDL hardware costs approximately $1 million, while open hardware ranges from $100 to $2,000 (pqac-00000034). The gravimetric doser would close a recognized gap by autonomously converting powders into robot-compatible, concentration-verified stock solutions, enabling SDLs to expand their reagent scope without requiring direct sub-milligram powder delivery into reaction vessels.

**Required specifications:** 5–500 mg; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; unattended 24/7 operation with error recovery; open scheduling API; auditable metadata; enclosures and interlocks.

The cost barrier to automated powder dispensing is substantial. Commercial liquid-handling workstations cost approximately $50,000–$60,000 (pqac-00000036), while specialized powder-dispensing systems from Chemspeed, Mettler-Toledo and similar manufacturers require "substantial capital investment" with additional costs for maintenance, laboratory space, and proprietary consumables (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000050). A documented, open-source powder doser at less than $5,000 BOM would represent a 10–100× cost reduction relative to commercial alternatives, democratizing a capability that remains uncommon in academic laboratories and virtually absent in low-resource settings.

**Required specifications:** 1 mg–5 g; ±0.1 mg readability; ≤5% RSD; simple calibration and maintenance; locally replaceable contact parts; open-source documentation, BOM, software and validation protocols.

### 3. Accuracy Requirements When Mass Is Recorded and Concentration Verified

A central question for the doser's value proposition is whether milligram-level gravimetric resolution is sufficient when downstream concentration correction is applied. The evidence strongly supports an affirmative answer for all six applications, with important caveats:

- **Gravimetric mass recording with solvent adjustment:** When the actual dispensed mass is recorded and solvent volume is calculated to reach the target molarity, preparation errors become traceable rather than unknown. The accuracy requirement shifts from "hit the target mass precisely" to "record the actual mass precisely" (pqac-00000016). A balance with 0.1 mg readability and ≤5% RSD dispensing performance is sufficient for this architecture.

- **Post-preparation concentration verification:** qNMR provides absolute concentration measurement with approximately 1% precision and 2% accuracy (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). LC-UV/MS relative purity can substantially misrepresent actual strength because it assumes all peaks sum to 100% (pqac-00000016). When qNMR or CLND is used for post-preparation verification, even larger initial dispensing errors are tolerable because the analytical measurement supersedes the gravimetric estimate.

Its milligram-to-gram operating range directly matches the most common stock-preparation, pre-formulation and prototyping workflows. The key enabling insight is that gravimetric feedback with mass recording, followed by solvent-volume adjustment or analytical concentration verification, relaxes the accuracy requirement from the sub-milligram level demanded by direct miniaturized reaction dosing to the ±5% level readily achievable by auger/vibratory gravimetric systems. At a target BOM of less than $5,000, the open-source doser would represent a 10–100× cost reduction relative to commercial alternatives, making automated powder handling accessible to academic core facilities, low-resource laboratories and modular SDL architectures worldwide."}

The gravimetric doser would close a recognized gap by autonomously converting powders into robot-compatible, concentration-verified stock solutions, enabling SDLs to expand their reagent scope without requiring direct sub-milligram powder delivery into reaction vessels.

---

### 5. Conclusions

The open-source gravimetric powder doser occupies a well-defined and underserved niche in pharmaceutical R&D automation: the **solid-to-stock-solution conversion** step that bridges bulk compound storage and downstream nanoliter-to-picoliter liquid dispensing. Its milligram-to-gram operating range directly matches the most common stock-preparation, pre-formulation and prototyping workflows. The key enabling insight is that gravimetric feedback with mass recording, followed by solvent-volume adjustment or analytical concentration verification, relaxes the accuracy requirement from the sub-milligram level demanded by direct miniaturized reaction dosing to the ±5% level readily achievable by auger/vibratory gravimetric systems. The doser does not compete with commercial sub-milligram platforms or ChemBead technology for direct 96/384-well HTE reaction setup, but it fills the upstream preparation gap that these platforms and self-driving laboratories currently address manually or avoid entirely. At a target BOM of less than $5,000, the open-source doser would represent a 10–100× cost reduction relative to commercial alternatives, making automated powder handling accessible to academic core facilities, low-resource laboratories and modular SDL architectures worldwide.

contexts.context: Automated solid-powder dispensing for medicinal-chemistry HTE must deliver small, reproducible doses across 96- and 384-well formats, while avoiding powder-flow problems such as bridging, static buildup, clogging, jamming, and inconsistent dosing. Conventional automated robots can provide sub-milligram accuracy and have demonstrated relative standard deviations typically below 5% across 96-well plates, but they may require substantial capital investment and laboratory space, and equipment malfunctions can cause downtime. ChemBeads address these issues by attaching uniformly distributed solid reagents to spherical, chemically inert glass beads. Their consistent physical properties and high flowability support reliable volumetric dispensing and help prevent common powder-handling failures. Automated platforms can dose multiple ChemBeads into microplates, including 96- and 384-well formats. For laboratories without robotic systems, calibrated fixed- or variable-volume scoops provide reproducible manual dosing without balance-based weighing; the delivered active amount can be calculated from pre-characterized loading. A parallel dispenser offers a lower-cost, higher-throughput alternative, using 96 calibrated holes designed for 3 mg of ChemBeads and achieving an error margin of ±5%. Multiple dispensers or premixed bead formulations can support dispensing multiple reagents per vial.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies automated solid-powder dispensing as a major bottleneck in medicinal-chemistry HTE. Workflows may require thousands of parallel reactions at sub-milligram quantities, including microgram-scale dosing, so reagent delivery must be accurate, reproducible, fast, and scalable. Even small dosing discrepancies can cause reaction failure or misleading results. Conventional approaches—manual microbalance weighing, spatula transfer, or preparing stock solutions—are labor-intensive, error-prone, and poorly suited to automation. Powder properties such as variable bulk density, particle-size heterogeneity, electrostatic charging, hygroscopicity, poor flow, air sensitivity, and cross-contamination create dose variability and irreproducible data. Dedicated powder-dispensing instruments improve accuracy but can be expensive, maintenance-intensive, and physically large. ChemBeads provide a solution by dry-coating active reagents onto inert carrier beads, converting difficult powders into uniform, free-flowing materials compatible with robotic or manual dispensing. Resonant acoustic mixing, or alternatives such as vortex mixing, enables their preparation. contexts.context: The excerpt addresses automated dispensing challenges for pharmaceutical reconstitution powders, although it does not specifically discuss high-throughput experimentation (HTE) in medicinal chemistry, dose ranges, numerical accuracy requirements, or the ChemBeads approach. It explains that spray-dried and bulk-lyophilised biological powders can be cohesive, adhesive, moisture-sensitive, shear-sensitive, aerated, and variable in density and flow. These properties make conventional volumetric filling unreliable: trapped air changes bulk density, powders may agglomerate or cake, and electrostatic forces can cause uncontrolled movement and adhesion to containers or equipment. Traditional augers and dosators may seize, shear or damage biological material, and cannot reliably control dispensed weight to pharmaceutical tolerances. Manual or analytical-balance systems can achieve weighing but are too slow for commercial throughput and unsuitable for aseptic isolators. The proposed Fill2Weight system combines high-speed gravimetric weighing with a powder-flow control valve, minimizing shear and handling powders across a wide flow range without change parts. Computer control provides self-tuning and compensation for changing powder properties, while multi-tracking can scale a single filling head for commercial applications. These principles may be relevant by analogy to HTE powder dispensing, but the excerpt provides no ChemBeads-specific design or performance data.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several challenges in automated dispensing of solid powders for medicinal-chemistry HTE. Reliable dosing depends on bead size, reagent physical properties, loading ratio, and preparation and storage conditions; deviations can affect powder flowability, dose accuracy, and reproducibility. Humidity and elevated temperature can cause recrystallization or reduced reagent loading, so ChemBeads should be stored in dry, controlled environments, potentially using desiccators or purge boxes. Reproducible scale-up is best supported by RAM instruments, which provide consistent dry-particle coating, although their cost and space requirements may limit access. Vortex mixing is a lower-resource alternative but can reduce consistency, throughput, and scalability. The ChemBeads strategy coats reagents physically onto inert glass beads without chemical modification or covalent bonding, preserving the reagent’s native chemical properties while enabling controlled dispensing. Fixed-volume and variable-volume scoops, as well as parallel dispensers, support rapid on-demand assembly of screening plates; multiple dispensers or premixed bead formulations can deliver several reagents per vial. The cited ChemOx application demonstrates dispensing into 96-well plates at reaction scales as low as 0.5 μmol per well. Standardized preparation protocols and batch characterization can improve accuracy, though complete inter-laboratory uniformity remains difficult.

contexts.context: Automated solid powder dispensing in HTE is difficult because powders vary substantially in physical behavior: they may be light, fluffy, heavy, electrostatically charged, hygroscopic, or granular. These properties complicate handling and increase measurement errors, so dispensing platforms must provide both accuracy and precision. Conventional systems have dose-range limitations. Chemspeed SWING and Mettler Toledo XPR are comparatively accurate for dispensing larger masses, but are unsuitable for small target quantities. Newer platforms, including Chemspeed FLEX, Chemspeed SWILE, Mettler Toledo CHRONECT, and Unchained Labs systems, can measure low- to sub-milligram quantities. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies poor powder flow, static-charge accumulation, and dose inconsistency as key barriers to automated solid dispensing in medicinal-chemistry HTE, where accurate microscale dosing is required for reliable automated synthesis. ChemBeads address these problems by coating chemically inert carrier beads—commonly glass, or polystyrene for biochemical applications—with fine reagent particles. Dry particle coating uses mechanical agitation, especially resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), to distribute reagent uniformly without covalent bonding, solvents, or binders. The resulting noncovalent adhesion is strong enough to preserve the reagent during storage and dispensing but weak enough to permit rapid, complete release in a compatible reaction solvent. This produces stable, homogeneous, free-flowing material suitable for manual and robotic dispensing. RAM improves reproducibility through rapid fluidization and dispersion, avoids dead zones and overheating, can be operated in sealed containers for moisture- or air-sensitive reagents, and scales from small tubes to one-liter bottles. Loading can be increased for higher-dose reagents such as inorganic bases or stoichiometric reagents, although excessive or uncoated material may impair flowability. contexts.context: Automated solid-powder dispensing in medicinal-chemistry HTE is difficult because native powders differ substantially in density, flowability, cohesiveness, static behavior, particle distribution, and hygroscopicity. These properties cause inconsistent transfer, dose variability, cross-contamination, irreproducible data, clogging, and robotic stalls, limiting unattended, scalable workflows. This is especially problematic when HTE requires representative neat powders or solid dosage forms for formulation, solubility, and solid-form studies. Commercial precision powder-handling systems can improve accuracy, but their cost, maintenance, and footprint restrict adoption; slurry dosing, wax encapsulation, capsules, and tablets have additional problems such as uneven distribution, clogging, or reagent degradation. AbbVie’s initial attempts to dispense more than 100 native solids produced weighing errors ranging from a few tenths to several hundredths of a percent and frequent instrument interruptions. ChemBeads address the problem by dry-coating finely powdered active reagents onto chemically inert glass beads, standardizing physical handling properties without compromising chemical integrity. The resulting free-flowing formulations support accurate, reproducible volumetric dispensing with standard robotic or manual tools, from nanomole to milligram scales. Bead surface area, size, and loading must be selected carefully: surface area controls capacity, while bead size supports uniform flow and prevents clogging. Typical loading is 0.5–20% w/w; approximately 5% w/w generally balances flowability, homogeneity, and automated dispense range.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes solid-powder handling as difficult because reconstitution powders are poorly flowing, sticky or cohesive, moisture-sensitive, shear-sensitive, and physically dynamic. Entrained air changes density and flow, while powders can aerate, settle, cake, agglomerate, or behave like solids, liquids, and occasionally gases. Hygroscopic powders often require low-humidity processing, which increases electrostatic charging; particles may move unpredictably and adhere to containers or equipment, creating contamination concerns in aseptic environments. Conventional volumetric filling is therefore unsuitable, and compression can improve repeatability but may damage biological materials and impair dissolution. Augers and dosators can seize, shear powders, and fail to achieve pharmaceutical weight tolerances. Existing workarounds include manual spatula-and-balance dispensing or slow automated dispensing over an analytical balance, but these approaches are labor-intensive, take roughly 30 seconds to several minutes per dispense, and are unsuitable for aseptic commercial operation. The cited Fill2Weight system instead uses high-speed gravimetric weighing, a powder-flow control valve, low-shear handling, and computer self-tuning to compensate for changing powder properties. contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss the specific challenges of handling solid powders, nor does it provide required dose ranges or dispensing-accuracy specifications. It does, however, describe general strategies that help current self-driving laboratories avoid or reduce difficult and hazardous material handling. Microfluidics and continuous-flow systems use small reagent volumes and compact reactors, improving heat, mass, and momentum transfer while reducing exposure to bulk chemicals. High-throughput experimentation similarly operates at micro- to nanomolar scales, limiting the quantity of material that must be handled; standardized wellplates also allow safety practices to be transferred across laboratories. Robotic arms and mobile robots reduce direct human contact with hazardous substances, but still require skilled personnel to monitor experiments, handle malfunctions, and intervene during emergencies. Relevant automation safeguards include constrained motion planning, collision detection, emergency stops, command preconditions, simulation or low-fidelity testing, and human-in-the-loop troubleshooting. ORGANA can identify unexpected outcomes and prompt user disambiguation, while RABIT monitors command sequences and enforces general and setup-specific rules. Thus, the passage supports the conclusion that SDLs often mitigate solids-related risks by minimizing quantities, using liquid-compatible micro/flow or HTE formats, and applying robotic and supervisory safeguards, but it supplies no quantitative powder-feeding accuracy or dose requirements.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several difficulties relevant to automated solid-powder handling. Spray-dried and bulk-lyophilized biological powders can be cohesive, adhesive, moisture-sensitive, shear-sensitive, and very poor-flowing. Their substantial entrained air—reported as 50–75% of dispensed material volume—makes bulk density and flow change with aeration, settling, and caking. Powders may therefore behave intermittently like solids, liquids, or gases, making ordinary volumetric dosing unreliable. Hygroscopic formulations often require low-humidity processing, which increases sensitivity to electrostatic charge; particles can move unpredictably and adhere to containers or equipment, creating contamination and process-control concerns. Compression can improve dose repeatability by removing voids, but may damage biological products and reduce dissolution. Conventional augers and dosators may seize, shear the powder, and fail to achieve pharmaceutical weight tolerances. Manual or analytical-balance-based dosing is slow and unsuitable for aseptic commercial operation. The excerpt does not specify an absolute dose range or numerical accuracy requirement. It describes Fill2Weight as using high-speed gravimetric weighing and a powder-flow-control valve, with computer self-tuning and compensation for changing powder properties; a single head can be multi-tracked for scale-up.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides empirical benchmarks for a validated quantitative 1H NMR method rather than prescribing a universal tolerance for stock-solution preparation. Across nine reference compounds, agreement between measured and declared or assumed strength was generally within approximately ±2%, indicating the method’s demonstrated accuracy. The precision table reports relative standard deviations of roughly 0.35–0.99% for individual operator/solution conditions, with overall averages around 1.36% and 1.32% for the two operators. For the BTMSB internal-standard stock solution, testing over 34 days found no meaningful time trend; daily averaged apparent strengths differed by no more than 1% from the overall average, and the solution was considered usable for up to one month at room temperature. These results suggest that when concentration is independently verified by qNMR, a practical acceptance expectation could be approximately 1% repeatability/precision and about 2% accuracy, subject to the specific assay and workflow. The excerpt does not directly address gravimetric preparation with exact dispensed-mass recording, solvent-volume adjustment, or post-preparation CLND or LC-UV/MS verification. Therefore, it cannot establish how much pipetting or weighing error is acceptable in those workflows; it only supplies a benchmark for the performance of the cited qNMR method and its internal-standard solution.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not establish a numerical accuracy or precision specification for stock-solution preparation. It supports a process-based conclusion: preparation should use accurate mass measurement and addition of the appropriate solvent volume, while the final concentration should be based on the recorded mass and adjusted to the target concentration. If exact dispensed mass and solvent volume are documented, preparation errors can be quantified or propagated rather than treated as unknown. When concentration is subsequently verified by qNMR, CLND, or LC-UV/MS, the analytical verification becomes the main control on the concentration assigned to the sample, so extreme gravimetric or volumetric precision may not be necessary provided preparation variability remains within the assay’s tolerance and the analytical method is sufficiently accurate and precise. The article particularly demonstrates that LC-UV relative purity can substantially misrepresent actual strength because it assumes all peaks sum to 100% and may omit or misweight species. Quantitative NMR gave a more reliable absolute-strength correction and improved agreement between library and pure-compound biological results. Thus, the relevant requirement is fit-for-purpose control and traceability, not an absolute universal weighing or pipetting tolerance; numerical tolerances would need to be set from the downstream bioassay and verification-method uncertainty.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specify a required weighing or dispensing tolerance for stock-solution preparation when the dispensed mass is recorded and solvent is adjusted to achieve the target concentration, nor does it provide requirements for CLND or LC-UV/MS verification. Its results indicate that the relevant requirement is the accuracy of the final, assigned concentration rather than an independently stringent preparation tolerance. Quantitative 1H NMR showed intrinsic measurement precision below 1%, while reproducibility across independently prepared solutions was better than 2% RSD. Accuracy testing gave results distributed within approximately ±2% around an average of about 102%, and manually pipetted preparation could improve both accuracy and precision to better than 1%. Thus, if exact mass and solvent volume are recorded sufficiently well, preparation uncertainty should be controlled to the intended concentration-accuracy target—approximately 1–2% based on this study. If concentration is subsequently verified by qNMR, CLND, or LC-UV/MS, the verification method can serve as the controlling concentration assignment, and larger initial dispensing errors may be acceptable provided they do not compromise solubility, stability, or assay validity and the measured concentration is used for downstream calculations. The paper specifically warns that concentrations inferred from assumed reaction or purification yields can be grossly unreliable.
contexts.question: What accuracy and precision are actually required for stock solution preparation in drug discovery when the exact dispensed mass is recorded and solvent volume is adjusted to reach target concentration, or when concentration is verified by qNMR, CLND, or LC-UV/MS afterwards?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes two miniaturized approaches relevant to preformulation and solid-form/formulation screening. In the powder-dispersion format, API consumption is approximately 0.1–15 mg per well in a 96-well plate, with the exact amount depending on the assay. This approach preserves the compound’s original solid form and can support thermodynamic solubility measurements if equilibrium is reached; it is therefore particularly relevant when maintaining or evaluating a crystalline API is important. The solvent-evaporation format uses substantially smaller quantities—about 10–40 μg per well—and can screen 96 formulations with duplicate measurements in 96-well plates within 1–2 days using HPLC. It is suitable for ranking diverse solubility-enhancing formulations, including viscous, semi-solid, and solid excipients, but may generate non-equilibrium systems such as supersaturated or amorphous formulations, different crystalline forms, or residual solvent. The excerpt does not provide a separate API dose range specifically labeled for polymorph, salt, or cocrystal screening; the cited solid-form literature is contextual rather than quantitative. Thus, the practical quantities reported here range from tens of micrograms per well for solvent-based screening to 0.1–15 mg per well for powder-dispersion assays.

It does establish general requirements relevant to powder dosing: powders have variable density and dynamic flow behavior, so gravimetric dosing is preferable to volumetric dosing where products are regulated by weight. The dispensing system must provide commercially practical speed, accurate and stable weighing, and control of cohesive, adhesive, moisture-sensitive, shear-sensitive powders without damaging biological material. It should minimize powder shear, avoid uncontrolled particulate contamination, and operate reliably in an aseptic isolator. For aseptic pharmaceutical use, equipment must tolerate aggressive decontamination such as hydrogen peroxide vapor; powder-contact components must be pharmaceutical-grade, suitable for autoclaving and direct product contact; and the design should preserve unidirectional airflow by maintaining a narrow footprint and avoiding turbulence. The described Fill2Weight system uses high-speed weighing, a flow-control valve, and computer-based self-tuning to compensate for changing powder properties. These points may inform requirements for the listed applications, but application-specific accuracy tolerances, batch-size criteria, validation expectations, and GMP rules are not provided in this excerpt.

DPI formulations are generally milligram-scale and may be supplied as unit-dose or multidose products. Filling approaches include volumetric systems (such as dosators, vacuum dosators, vacuum drums, and tamp fillers) and gravimetric systems (including microdosing, vacuum drum, and membrane filling). Standard dosator equipment can fill approximately 10–500 mg with very low relative standard deviation (%RSD). In one lactose-based salbutamol sulfate example, the best reported condition used a dosing chamber-to-powder-layer compression ratio of 1:2, achieving a fine particle fraction (FPF) of 12% and filling %RSD below 0.8%. Vacuum drum filling minimizes powder compression and its effect on powder properties, and is particularly useful for cohesive or low-dose formulations because it reduces fill-weight variability. Dose delivery depends on vacuum pressure, drum-bore size, stirrer type and speed, and powder properties. For inhalation blend prototyping, the excerpt emphasizes optimizing blending, milling, particle size, mixing, and aerosol performance; however, it gives no explicit mass-accuracy target, GMP specification, or requirements applicable to 3D-printed tablets or personalized compounding.
